title: Adverbial participles
objectives: I can explain what an adverbial participle is and why it is a form of the verb, not an adverb.
I can form imperfective adverbial participles such as 'чита́ючи', 'пи́шучи' and 'ідучи́' from the 'вони́' form, and reflexive ones in '-чись'.
I can form perfective adverbial participles such as 'прочита́вши', 'прийшо́вши' and 'поверну́вшись' from the masculine past.
I can use an adverbial participle only when its action belongs to the subject of the main verb, set it off with commas, and replace it with 'коли́' or 'і' in conversation.
I can tell and follow a story about a hike in the mountains in a written style.

vocabulary.note: 'Мандру́ю', 'мандру́єш', 'мандру́ють': '-ува-' becomes '-у-' in the present, as in 'працюва́ти'. It means to travel for the pleasure of the journey, often on foot; 'подорожува́ти' is the general word for traveling. It has no perfective partner in everyday use.

example.target: Улі́тку ми лю́бимо мандрува́ти в гора́х.
example.source: In summer we love hiking in the mountains.
example.source_literal: In-summer we love to-wander in mountains.

vocabulary.note: A trip told as an adventure: a hike, a walk of several days or a long journey. It is built from 'мандрува́ти'. Genitive plural 'мандрі́вок'.

example.source: We're planning a hike in the Carpathians.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'лі́су'; plural 'ліси́'. 'До лі́су' is into the forest, 'з лі́су' out of it, and 'че́рез ліс' through it.

example.target: Ми ви́йшли з лі́су й поба́чили рі́чку.
example.source: We came out of the forest and saw a river.
example.source_literal: We went-out from forest and saw river.

vocabulary.note: The everyday word for a river. Before the ending '-і' its 'к' becomes 'ц': 'у рі́чці', in the river; 'на рі́чці', on the river. Genitive plural 'рі́чок'.

example.source: The tent stands by the river.

vocabulary.note: A narrow path for walking, in a forest, a park or the mountains. 'На сте́жці': on the path, with 'к' becoming 'ц' before '-і'. Genitive plural 'сте́жок'.

example.source: This path goes through the forest.

vocabulary.note: The highest point of a mountain. 'На верши́ні': at the summit; 'на верши́ну': up to the summit.
Genitive 'гори́', accusative 'го́ру', locative 'на горі́'; plural 'го́ри'. 'У гора́х' is in the mountains and 'в го́ри' to the mountains, so 'Ми ї́демо в го́ри.' means 'We're going to the mountains.'

example.target: Гове́рла ви́ща за всі і́нші го́ри Украї́ни.
example.source: Hoverla is higher than all the other mountains of Ukraine.
example.source_literal: Hoverla higher than all other mountains of-Ukraine.

example.target: У на́шому наме́ті є мі́сце для трьох.
example.source: There is room for three in our tent.
example.source_literal: In our tent is place for three.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'рюкзака́': the stress moves to the ending in every other form. 'У рюкзаку́': in the backpack, with '-у' as in 'на літаку́'.
Built from 'вого́нь', fire, and the suffix '-ище', which here names a place: the place where a fire burns. 'Бі́ля вогни́ща': by the campfire.

example.source: In the evening we sat by the campfire.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'краєви́ду'. It joins 'край', land, and 'вид', view, the word that also means aspect in grammar. It names a wide view of the land, often seen from a high place.

example.target: З верши́ни ми ба́чили га́рний краєви́д.
example.source: From the summit we saw a beautiful view.

vocabulary.note: 'Підніма́юся', 'підніма́єшся', 'підніма́ються'. The perfective partner is 'підня́тися', past 'підня́вся'. Without '-ся', 'підніма́ти' is to lift. The place reached takes 'на' and the accusative: 'підніма́тися на го́ру', 'на п’я́тий по́верх'.

example.source: We are going up to the fifth floor.

vocabulary.note: 'Спуска́юся', 'спуска́єшся'. The perfective partner is 'спусти́тися', past 'спусти́вся', 'спусти́лися'. The starting point takes 'з' and the genitive: 'спуска́тися з гори́'.

example.target: Спуска́тися з гори́ ча́сто ва́жче, ніж підніма́тися.
example.source: Going down a mountain is often harder than going up.
example.source_literal: To-go-down from mountain often harder, than to-go-up.

vocabulary.note: Future 'відпочи́ну', 'відпочи́неш', on a stem with an 'н' that the infinitive does not show. The imperfective partner is 'відпочива́ти'.
Future 'заблука́ю', 'заблука́єш'. It names one completed event and has no common imperfective partner; 'блука́ти', without the prefix, is to wander about with no clear way.

example.target: Рік тому́ ми заблука́ли в гора́х.
example.source: A year ago we got lost in the mountains.
example.source_literal: Year ago we got-lost in mountains.

vocabulary.note: Future 'помі́чу', 'помі́тиш', 'помі́тять': 'т' becomes 'ч' in the 'я' form only. The imperfective partner is 'поміча́ти'.

example.source: I noticed a path by the river.

vocabulary.source: to look around, to look back
vocabulary.note: 'Озира́юся', 'озира́єшся'. The perfective partner is 'озирну́тися', to look back once. With 'на' and the accusative it means to look back at something: 'озира́тися на го́ри'.

example.source: She walked on, often looking back.

vocabulary.note: The adverb of 'ти́хий', quiet. In 'Тут ти́хо.' (It is quiet here) the same word is a predicative word, the predicate of a sentence without a subject.

example.source: Speak quietly, because everyone is asleep.

vocabulary.note: 'Посміха́юся', 'посміха́єшся'. The perfective partner is 'посміхну́тися', to give one smile. The person smiled at is in the dative: 'посміха́тися дру́гові'.

dialogues.title: Packing for the mountains
dialogues.context: Taras and Sam are planning a weekend hike to Hoverla in the Carpathians and are packing their backpacks at Taras's apartment. They say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Се́ме, що ти бере́ш у го́ри?
lines.source: Sam, what are you taking to the mountains?
lines.source_literal: Sam, what you take to mountains?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Во́ду, хліб і сир. Хліб і сир я купи́в, ідучи́ з робо́ти.
lines.source: Water, bread and cheese. I bought the bread and cheese on my way home from work.
lines.source_literal: Water, bread and cheese. Bread and cheese I bought, going from work.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́бре. А наме́т я візьму́ свій. Він стари́й, але́ до́брий.
lines.source: Good. And I'll bring my own tent. It's old, but it's a good one.
lines.source_literal: Good. And tent I will-take own. It old, but good.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Скі́льки годи́н тре́ба йти до верши́ни?
lines.source: How many hours does it take to walk to the summit?
lines.source_literal: How-many of-hours necessary to-go to summit?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Прибли́зно три годи́ни, якщо́ ми не заблука́ємо.
lines.source: About three hours, if we don't get lost.
lines.source_literal: Approximately three hours, if we not will-get-lost.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А ми мо́жемо заблука́ти? Я ду́мав, що там є сте́жка.
lines.source: Can we get lost? I thought there was a path.
lines.source_literal: And we can to-get-lost? I thought, that there is path.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Є. Але́ мину́лого лі́та там заблука́в мій знайо́мий, ду́маючи, що до́бре зна́є го́ри.
lines.source: There is. But last summer someone I know got lost there, thinking he knew the mountains well.
lines.source_literal: Is. But of-last of-summer there got-lost my acquaintance, thinking, that well knows mountains.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Тоді́ ти йди пе́ред мно́ю, а я піду́ за тобо́ю.
lines.source: Then you go in front, and I'll follow you.
lines.source_literal: Then you go in-front-of me, and I will-go behind you.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́бре. І візьми́ те́плу ку́ртку, бо в гора́х уночі́ ду́же хо́лодно.
lines.source: Fine. And take a warm jacket, because it's very cold in the mountains at night.
lines.source_literal: Fine. And take warm jacket, because in mountains at-night very cold.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я ще ніко́ли не спав у наме́ті.
lines.source: I've never slept in a tent before.
lines.source_literal: I still never not slept in tent.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Не бі́йся. Пі́сля тако́го дня ти бу́деш спа́ти, як дити́на.
lines.source: Don't worry. After a day like that you'll sleep like a baby.
lines.source_literal: Not fear. After such of-day you will sleep, like child.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Тоді́ до субо́ти! Я бу́ду на вокза́лі о шо́стій.
lines.source: Until Saturday, then! I'll be at the station at six.
lines.source_literal: Then until Saturday! I will-be on station at sixth.

dialogues.title: Lost in the forest
dialogues.context: On Monday Olena meets Oksana at Andrii's café and tells her about her weekend walk in a forest outside Kyiv. The two friends say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Оле́но, як твої́ вихідні́? Ти ходи́ла в ліс?
lines.source: Olena, how was your weekend? Did you go to the forest?
lines.source_literal: Olena, how your weekend? You went to forest?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ходи́ла. І, пра́вду ка́жучи, я там заблука́ла!
lines.source: I did. And to tell the truth, I got lost there!
lines.source_literal: Went. And, truth saying, I there got-lost!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ти заблука́ла? Але́ ти так до́бре зна́єш той ліс!
lines.source: You got lost? But you know that forest so well!
lines.source_literal: You got-lost? But you so well know that forest!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Зна́ю. Я йшла вздовж рі́чки й ду́мала про робо́ту.
lines.source: I know. I was walking along the river, thinking about work.
lines.source_literal: I-know. I went along river and thought about work.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: І не помі́тила, куди́ йдеш?
lines.source: And you didn't notice where you were going?
lines.source_literal: And not noticed, where-to you-go?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Так. Ра́птом я помі́тила, що сте́жки вже нема́є.
lines.source: Right. Suddenly I noticed that the path wasn't there anymore.
lines.source_literal: Yes. Suddenly I noticed, that of-path already there-is-not.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А телефо́н? Ти не могла́ подзвони́ти?
lines.source: What about your phone? Couldn't you call someone?
lines.source_literal: And phone? You not could to-phone?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Телефо́н там не працюва́в.
lines.source: My phone didn't work there.
lines.source_literal: Phone there not worked.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: І що ти зроби́ла?
lines.source: So what did you do?
lines.source_literal: And what you did?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Споча́тку я ду́же боя́лася. Але́ по́тім я ти́хо стоя́ла й слу́хала. Десь бли́зько була́ рі́чка: я її́ чу́ла!
lines.source: At first I was very scared. But then I stood still and listened. The river was somewhere close: I could hear it!
lines.source_literal: At-first I very was-afraid. But then I quietly stood and listened. Somewhere near was river: I it heard!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: І ти пішла́ до рі́чки?
lines.source: And you went to the river?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Так. Дійшо́вши до рі́чки, я знайшла́ сте́жку. А додо́му я йшла, ча́сто озира́ючись.
lines.source: Yes. When I reached the river, I found the path. And all the way home I kept looking back.
lines.source_literal: Yes. Having-reached to river, I found path. And home I went, often looking-around.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Насту́пної субо́ти я піду́ з тобо́ю.
lines.source: Next Saturday I'll go with you.
lines.source_literal: Of-next of-Saturday I will-go with you.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Дя́кую! Ра́зом ми не заблука́ємо.
lines.source: Thank you! Together we won't get lost.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! Together we not will-get-lost.

grammar.title: What an adverbial participle is, and the imperfective form in '-чи'
grammar.explanation:
An adverbial participle is a form of the verb that adds a second action to a sentence without a second subject. It depends on the main verb and says when, how or in what situation the main action happens, the job an adverb does: 'Ідучи́ додо́му, я співа́в.' (I sang as I walked home). English does something similar with '-ing' and 'having': 'walking home', 'having read the book'.

The Ukrainian name is 'дієприслі́вник'. It joins the names of two parts of speech, 'дієсло́во', verb, and 'прислі́вник', adverb, because the form does an adverb's job. It is still a form of the verb, not an adverb:

- it keeps the verb's aspect: an imperfective verb gives an imperfective form, and a perfective verb a perfective one
- it takes the same objects and cases as the verb: 'чита́ти кни́гу', 'чита́ючи кни́гу' (reading the book), with 'кни́гу' in the accusative both times
- it keeps the '-ся' of a reflexive verb

It never changes: it has no person, no gender, no number and no tense, and the main verb supplies all of them. 'Ідучи́ додо́му, я співа́ю.', 'Ідучи́ додо́му, вона́ співа́ла.' and 'Ідучи́ додо́му, ми бу́демо співа́ти.' all use the same form. This sets it apart from the passive participles of the previous unit, such as 'прочи́таний', which decline like adjectives and agree with a noun.

There are two kinds, one for each aspect. The imperfective kind ends in '-чи' and names an action that happens at the same time as the main verb. The perfective kind ends in '-ши' and names an action completed before it. This note builds the first kind; the next note builds the second.

The imperfective form is built on the 'вони́' form of the present tense: drop the ending '-ть' and add '-чи'. Only imperfective verbs have a present, so only they have this form.

- first conjugation: 'чита́ють', 'чита́ючи'; 'пи́шуть', 'пи́шучи'; 'іду́ть', 'ідучи́'
- second conjugation: 'ба́чать', 'ба́чачи'; 'сидя́ть', 'сидячи́'

So the first conjugation gives '-учи' or '-ючи', and the second gives '-ачи' or '-ячи'. Because the base is the 'вони́' form, everything in that form is kept: 'писа́ти' has 'ш' in 'пи́шуть', so the adverbial participle is 'пи́шучи'.

A reflexive verb builds the form without '-ся' and then adds the short '-сь': 'озира́ються', 'озира́ючи', 'озира́ючись' (looking around).

Most forms keep the stress of the 'вони́' form: 'чита́ють', 'чита́ючи'; 'ї́дуть', 'ї́дучи'. Where the 'вони́' form stresses its ending, the stress moves to '-чи': 'іду́ть', 'ідучи́'; 'несу́ть', 'несучи́'; 'сидя́ть', 'сидячи́'.

One verb is different. 'Бу́ти' has no present forms of its own apart from 'є', so it builds its adverbial participle on the future 'бу́дуть': 'бу́дучи', being. The noun after it is in the instrumental, as after 'бу́ти': 'Бу́дучи студе́нткою, Оле́на бага́то мандрува́ла.' (As a student, Olena traveled a lot).

examples.source: I sang as I walked home.
Sam writes fast while listening to the teacher.

examples.target: Підніма́ючись на го́ру, ми ча́сто відпочива́ли.
examples.source: We rested often as we climbed the mountain.
examples.source_literal: Going-up onto mountain, we often rested.

examples.source: Oksana read a book while she traveled by train.
As a student, Olena traveled a lot.

grammar.title: The perfective form in '-ши': one action before another
grammar.explanation:
The perfective adverbial participle names an action that is completed before the action of the main verb: 'Прочита́вши кни́гу, Сем посміхну́вся.' (After reading the book, Sam smiled). English says 'having read' or 'after reading'; Ukrainian uses one word.

It is built on the masculine past form, the one used with 'він': add '-ши'.

- a past in '-в' gives '-вши': 'прочита́в', 'прочита́вши'; 'сказа́в', 'сказа́вши'; 'прийшо́в', 'прийшо́вши'
- a past that ends in another consonant adds '-ши' directly: 'ви́ріс', 'ви́рісши' (having grown up)

The stress stays where the masculine past has it: 'прийшо́в', 'прийшо́вши'; 'ви́йшов', 'ви́йшовши'. A past of one syllable, such as 'взяв', gains a syllable, and the mark goes on its vowel: 'взя́вши'.

A reflexive verb drops '-ся' from the past, adds '-ши' and then the short '-сь', as the imperfective kind does: 'поверну́вся', 'поверну́вши', 'поверну́вшись' (having come back); 'підня́вся', 'підня́вшись' (having climbed).

The form in '-вши' comes from perfective verbs, because an action finished before another one is a completed whole. Imperfective verbs can also take '-вши' ('чита́вши', having been reading), but that form is rare and belongs to old written style; this course does not use it.

Like the imperfective kind, it has no tense of its own. The main verb sets the time, and the participle's action simply comes first, in the past or in the future: 'Поверну́вшись додо́му, я тобі́ подзвоню́.' (When I get back home, I'll call you).

With 'не' before it, an adverbial participle of either aspect means 'without doing': 'не сказа́вши', without having said, and 'не ка́жучи', without saying. It then usually follows the main verb. With 'нічо́го' it makes the double negative that Ukrainian requires with every negative pronoun: 'Він пішо́в, нічо́го не сказа́вши.' (He left without saying anything).

examples.source: After reading the book, Sam smiled.

examples.target: Узя́вши рюкза́к, Тара́с ви́йшов із до́му.
examples.source: Taras picked up his backpack and left the house.
examples.source_literal: Having-taken backpack, Taras went-out from house.

examples.target: Ви́рісши в Ки́єві, Оле́на до́бре зна́є це мі́сто.
examples.source: Having grown up in Kyiv, Olena knows the city well.
examples.source_literal: Having-grown-up in Kyiv, Olena well knows this city.

examples.source: When I get back home, I'll call you.
He left without saying anything.

grammar.title: One subject for both actions, and the commas
grammar.explanation:
The person or thing that does the action of an adverbial participle is always the subject of the main verb. In 'Ми́ючи ча́шки, Окса́на співа́ла.' (Oksana sang as she washed the cups) the one washing is Oksana, because she is the subject of 'співа́ла'. The form shows no person, so the sentence has no other way to say who does it.

When the two actions have different subjects, an adverbial participle cannot be used. Ukrainian then uses a clause with its own subject and verb, opened by 'коли́' (when, while), 'по́ки' (while) or 'як ті́льки' (as soon as), from the unit on telling a story: 'Коли́ Окса́на ми́ла ча́шки, Тара́с чита́в.' (While Oksana was washing the cups, Taras was reading). Before you use the form, check that the subject of the main verb does both actions.

An adverbial participle, alone or with the words that belong to it (its object, its place, its time), is set off by commas from the rest of the sentence, wherever it stands:

- before the main clause: 'Ми́ючи ча́шки, Окса́на співа́ла.'
- after it: 'Оле́на ти́хо співа́ла, ідучи́ вздовж рі́чки.'
- in the middle, with a comma on each side: 'Тара́с, озира́ючись, ішо́в до лі́су.'

The words that belong to the participle stay inside the commas with it, so the commas show the reader where the second action begins and ends. A comma counts as a pause for euphony, which is why 'ідучи́' keeps its 'і' after a comma.

Three forms are the exception. 'Сидячи́', 'стоячи́' and 'лежачи́', standing alone after the verb, only say how the body is placed, the way an adverb says how something is done, and they take no comma: 'Він лю́бить чита́ти лежачи́.' (He likes to read lying down). With words of their own they follow the rule again: 'Окса́на чита́є, сидячи́ на балко́ні.'

rows: Oksana sang as she washed the cups.
After finishing work, Olena went home.
Коли́ Окса́на ми́ла ча́шки, Тара́с чита́в.
when Oksana washed cups, Taras read
While Oksana was washing the cups, Taras was reading.
Taras walked to the forest, looking back.
Оле́на ти́хо співа́ла, ідучи́ вздовж рі́чки.
Olena quietly sang, going along river
Olena sang quietly as she walked along the river.
He likes to read lying down.

examples.source: Sam smiled as he listened to Taras.
Sam smiled while Taras sang.

examples.target: Окса́на, поверну́вшись із робо́ти, подзвони́ла ма́мі.
examples.source: After she got back from work, Oksana called her mom.
examples.source_literal: Oksana, having-returned from work, phoned to-mom.

examples.source: Sam likes to work standing up.

grammar.title: Written and spoken style: the adverbial participle, 'коли́' and 'і'
grammar.explanation:
Adverbial participles belong mainly to written Ukrainian: stories, news, letters and instructions. They pack two actions into one sentence with one subject, which suits careful writing. In everyday conversation Ukrainians usually say the same thing in one of two other ways:

- a clause with 'коли́' and its own verb: 'Коли́ я йшов до вокза́лу, я зустрі́в Оле́ну.' in place of 'Ідучи́ до вокза́лу, я зустрі́в Оле́ну.'
- two verbs joined by 'і': 'Тара́с прийшо́в додо́му й подзвони́в ма́мі.' in place of 'Прийшо́вши додо́му, Тара́с подзвони́в ма́мі.'

Keep the aspect when you change the form: an imperfective participle becomes an imperfective verb ('ідучи́', 'йшов'), and a perfective participle becomes a perfective verb ('прийшо́вши', 'прийшо́в').

Conversation still uses a few adverbial participles:

- short, everyday ones such as 'ідучи́': 'Я купи́в хліб, ідучи́ з робо́ти.' (I bought bread on my way home from work)
- 'сидячи́', 'стоячи́' and 'лежачи́', which say how the body is placed
- fixed phrases, above all 'пра́вду ка́жучи', to tell the truth, literally 'truth saying', which opens a sentence and is set off by a comma

When you write a story, mix the forms: an adverbial participle for the second action in some sentences, 'коли́' or 'і' in others, as the two readings of this unit do. A text with a participle in every sentence sounds heavy, even in writing.

rows: Ідучи́ до вокза́лу, я зустрі́в Оле́ну.
going to station, I met Olena
On my way to the station, I met Olena.
Коли́ я йшов до вокза́лу, я зустрі́в Оле́ну.
when I went to station, I met Olena
When I was walking to the station, I met Olena.
When Taras got home, he called his mom.
Тара́с прийшо́в додо́му й подзвони́в ма́мі.
Taras came home and phoned to-mom
Taras came home and called his mom.
Пра́вду ка́жучи, я ніко́ли не був у гора́х.
truth saying, I never not was in mountains
To tell the truth, I've never been to the mountains.

examples.target: Подзвони́вши Оле́ні, Окса́на пішла́ в кафе́.
examples.source: After calling Olena, Oksana went to the café.
examples.source_literal: Having-phoned to-Olena, Oksana went to café.

examples.target: Окса́на подзвони́ла Оле́ні й пішла́ в кафе́.
examples.source: Oksana called Olena and went to the café.
examples.source_literal: Oksana phoned to-Olena and went to café.

examples.target: Стоячи́ в авто́бусі, я чита́ю нови́ни.
examples.source: I read the news standing on the bus.
examples.source_literal: Standing in bus, I read news.

examples.target: Коли́ я стою́ в авто́бусі, я чита́ю нови́ни.
examples.source: When I'm standing on the bus, I read the news.
examples.source_literal: When I stand in bus, I read news.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: ідучи́, ї́дучи, посміха́ючись and поверну́вшись
grammar.explanation:
Every new form and word of this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The points below are the ones that the adverbial participles and the hiking words bring up.

The ending '-чи' is said [t͡ʃɪ]: 'ч' is hard here, and 'и' is the [ɪ] of the alphabet units. 'Чита́ючи' is [t͡ʃɪˈtɑjut͡ʃɪ], and its 'ю' after the vowel 'а' gives [ju].

'Ідучи́' and 'ї́дучи' differ in their first letter and in their stress. 'І' is a plain [i], but 'ї' is always [ji], so 'ї́дучи' [ˈjidut͡ʃɪ] begins with a [j]. Each keeps the stress pattern of its 'вони́' form: 'іду́ть' stresses the ending, so the stress moves to '-чи' [iduˈt͡ʃɪ], while 'ї́дуть' stresses the stem, and so does 'ї́дучи'. Like 'іти́' and 'йти', the form 'ідучи́' becomes 'йдучи́' after a word that ends in a vowel, by the euphony rule of the unit on stress, and keeps 'і' at the start of a sentence, after a consonant and after a comma.

The suffix '-сь' ends in a soft [sʲ], which the soft sign shows: 'посміха́ючись' [pɔsmʲiˈxɑjut͡ʃɪsʲ], smiling, from 'посміха́тися'. In the other forms of a reflexive verb you may meet '-ся' or '-сь' after a vowel, but an adverbial participle takes '-сь'.

In every form in '-вши' the 'в' stands before a consonant, so it is said [w], as in 'вже': 'прочита́вши' [prɔt͡ʃɪˈtɑwʃɪ], 'поверну́вшись' [pɔʋɛrˈnuwʃɪsʲ]. The first 'в' of 'поверну́вшись' stands before a vowel and is the usual [ʋ].

In 'ви́рісши' the 'с' meets 'ш', and the tongue takes the position of 'ш' early, so 'сш' is one long [ʃː], like the doubled consonant of 'життя́': [ˈʋɪrʲiʃːɪ]. The spelling keeps 'с', which shows the past 'ви́ріс' inside the form.

The new words:

- 'рюкза́к' [rʲuɡˈzɑk]: the voiceless 'к' becomes a voiced [ɡ] before the voiced 'з', as in 'вокза́л'; the stress moves to the ending in the other forms: 'рюкзака́', 'у рюкзаку́'
- 'краєви́д' [krɑjɛˈʋɪd]: 'є' after a vowel is [jɛ], and the final 'д' stays voiced
- 'вогни́ще' [ʋɔɦˈnɪʃt͡ʃɛ]: 'щ' is the two sounds [ʃt͡ʃ]
- 'мандрі́вка' [mɑnˈdrʲiwkɑ]: 'в' before 'к' is [w]
- 'сте́жка' [ˈstɛʒkɑ]: 'ж' stays voiced before the voiceless 'к', because Ukrainian keeps voiced consonants voiced
- 'сте́жка' and 'рі́чка': 'к' becomes 'ц' before the ending '-і', 'на сте́жці', 'у рі́чці', as in 'рука́', 'у руці́'
- 'помі́тити': 'т' becomes 'ч' in the 'я' form only, 'помі́чу', 'помі́тиш', as in 'леті́ти', 'лечу́'
- 'гора́': the stress moves, 'гора́', 'на горі́', but 'на го́ру' and the plural 'го́ри'
- 'підніма́ється', 'спуска́ються': '-ться' is said [t͡sʲːɑ], a long soft [t͡sʲ]

examples.source: We drove home, singing quietly.
Taras walked along, smiling.

examples.target: Поверну́вшись із гір, Сем купи́в нови́й рюкза́к.
examples.source: After coming back from the mountains, Sam bought a new backpack.
examples.source_literal: Having-returned from mountains, Sam bought new backpack.

examples.source: We noticed a tent on the path.

culture.title: The Carpathians, Hoverla and the polonyny
culture.text:
The Ukrainian Carpathians, 'Карпа́ти', are a range of wooded mountains in the west of the country. They are not very high, so they are a place for walking rather than for climbing with ropes: most routes are long marked paths through beech and fir forest and over open ridges. The highest summit is 'Гове́рла', 2,061 meters high, on the ridge called 'Чорного́ра', literally 'black mountain'. Many Ukrainians climb Hoverla at least once in their lives. On a summer weekend hundreds of people walk up the same path, and many of them carry the blue and yellow national flag to the summit.

Above the forest lie high mountain meadows without trees, called 'полони́ни'. In summer shepherds bring their sheep and cows up to them and stay there for months, making cheese such as 'бри́нза', a salty sheep's cheese.

The people of the highest part of the Carpathians are the Hutsuls, 'гуцу́ли', known for their carved wood, their embroidered clothes and a wooden horn called 'трембі́та', three meters or more in length, whose sound carries far across the valleys. Shepherds once used it to send signals from the polonyny.

Experienced hikers in the Carpathians keep a few rules:

- stay on the marked path: painted stripes on trees and stones show the route
- set off early, because the weather in the mountains changes quickly and storms are common on summer afternoons
- tell someone the route before you go

A hike, 'мандрі́вка', usually ends by a campfire, 'вогни́ще', with tea, songs and stories, and stories about getting lost are a favorite.

paragraphs.target: Цього́ лі́та ми з Тара́сом пої́хали в Карпа́ти. Я до́вго мрі́яв підня́тися на Гове́рлу, найви́щу го́ру Украї́ни.
paragraphs.source: This summer Taras and I went to the Carpathians. For a long time I had dreamed of climbing Hoverla, the highest mountain in Ukraine.
paragraphs.source_literal: Of-this of-summer we with Taras went to Carpathians. I long dreamed to-climb onto Hoverla, highest mountain of-Ukraine.

paragraphs.target: Приї́хавши в го́ри уве́чері, ми спа́ли в наме́ті бі́ля рі́чки. Ми ви́йшли ду́же ра́но.
paragraphs.source: We arrived in the mountains in the evening and slept in a tent by a river. We set off very early.
paragraphs.source_literal: Having-arrived to mountains in-evening, we slept in tent near river. We went-out very early.

paragraphs.target: Сте́жка йшла че́рез ліс, і ми пові́льно підніма́лися, відпочива́ючи ко́жну годи́ну. Тара́с ішо́в пе́ред мно́ю, ти́хо співа́ючи.
paragraphs.source: The path went through the forest, and we climbed slowly, resting every hour. Taras walked ahead of me, singing quietly.
paragraphs.source_literal: Path went through forest, and we slowly went-up, resting every hour. Taras went in-front-of me, quietly singing.

paragraphs.target: Ви́йшовши з лі́су, ми поба́чили верши́ну. Вона́ була́ ще дале́ко, і ми йшли ду́же пові́льно.
paragraphs.source: When we came out of the forest, we saw the summit. It was still far away, and we walked very slowly.
paragraphs.source_literal: Having-gone-out from forest, we saw summit. It was still far, and we went very slowly.

paragraphs.target: Підня́вшись на верши́ну, ми до́вго відпочива́ли. Краєви́д був таки́й га́рний, що ми забу́ли про все.
paragraphs.source: Having reached the summit, we rested for a long time. The view was so beautiful that we forgot about everything.
paragraphs.source_literal: Having-climbed onto summit, we long rested. View was so beautiful, that we forgot about all.

paragraphs.target: Спуска́ючись, я ча́сто озира́вся на Гове́рлу. Поверну́вшись до наме́ту, ми сиді́ли бі́ля вогни́ща до но́чі й пили́ чай.
paragraphs.source: On the way down, I often looked back at Hoverla. Back at the tent, we sat by the campfire until night and drank tea.
paragraphs.source_literal: Going-down, I often looked-around at Hoverla. Having-returned to tent, we sat near campfire until night and drank tea.

paragraphs.target: Насту́пного дня ми пої́хали додо́му, обіця́ючи собі́ поверну́тися.
paragraphs.source: The next day we went home, promising ourselves that we would come back.
paragraphs.source_literal: Of-next of-day we went home, promising to-self to-return.

questions.prompt: Where did the narrator and Taras spend their first night in the mountains?
choices: In a hotel in a mountain village
In a tent by a river
In a house at the foot of Hoverla
questions.explanation: 'Приї́хавши в го́ри уве́чері, ми спа́ли в наме́ті бі́ля рі́чки.' The perfective participle 'приї́хавши' says that they arrived first and then slept.

questions.prompt: What was Taras doing while he walked ahead of the narrator?
choices: He was looking back at the forest.
He was talking on the phone.
He was singing quietly.
questions.explanation: 'Тара́с ішо́в пе́ред мно́ю, ти́хо співа́ючи.' The imperfective participle 'співа́ючи' names an action at the same time as 'ішо́в'.

questions.prompt: When did they see the summit?
choices: As soon as they came out of the forest
Before they set off in the morning
Only when they reached the top
questions.explanation: 'Ви́йшовши з лі́су, ми поба́чили верши́ну.' The action of 'ви́йшовши' is completed before 'поба́чили'.

questions.prompt: Who kept looking back at Hoverla on the way down?
choices: Taras
The narrator
Both of them
questions.explanation: 'Спуска́ючись, я ча́сто озира́вся на Гове́рлу.' The participle belongs to the subject 'я', the narrator who tells the story.

paragraphs.target: Восени́ оди́н чолові́к ішо́в че́рез ліс до ха́ти свого́ дру́га. Ду́маючи про своє́ життя́, він не помі́тив, що сте́жка закі́нчилася. Уже́ темні́ло.
paragraphs.source: One autumn a man was walking through a forest to his friend's house. Thinking about his life, he did not notice that the path had come to an end. It was already getting dark.
paragraphs.source_literal: In-autumn one man went through forest to house of-own of-friend. Thinking about own life, he not noticed, that path ended. Already it-was-getting-dark.

paragraphs.target: Поба́чивши, що заблука́в, чолові́к не знав, що роби́ти. Він до́вго ходи́в туди́ й сюди́, але́ не міг знайти́ сте́жку.
paragraphs.source: When he saw that he was lost, the man did not know what to do. For a long time he walked back and forth, but he could not find the path.
paragraphs.source_literal: Having-seen, that got-lost, man not knew, what to-do. He long walked there and here, but not could to-find path.

paragraphs.target: Ра́птом він помі́тив вого́нь. Ідучи́ на вого́нь, він ти́хо співа́в, щоб не боя́тися. Бі́ля вогни́ща сиді́ла стара́ жі́нка.
paragraphs.source: Suddenly he noticed a fire. As he walked toward the fire, he sang quietly so as not to be afraid. An old woman was sitting by the campfire.
paragraphs.source_literal: Suddenly he noticed fire. Going toward fire, he quietly sang, so-that not to-be-afraid. Near campfire sat old woman.

paragraphs.target: Жі́нка посміхну́лася й сказа́ла: «Ви не заблука́ли. Ха́та ва́шого дру́га за рі́чкою».
paragraphs.source: The woman smiled and said: "You are not lost. Your friend's house is across the river."
paragraphs.source_literal: Woman smiled and said: "You not got-lost. House of-your of-friend behind river."

paragraphs.target: Сказа́вши «дя́кую», чолові́к пішо́в до рі́чки. Перейшо́вши че́рез рі́чку, він поба́чив сві́тло у вікні́ свого́ дру́га.
paragraphs.source: The man said thank you and went to the river. Once he had crossed the river, he saw the light in his friend's window.
paragraphs.source_literal: Having-said "I-thank", man went to river. Having-crossed across river, he saw light in window of-own of-friend.

paragraphs.target: Він озирну́вся, але́ жі́нки й вогни́ща там уже́ не було́.
paragraphs.source: He looked back, but the woman and the fire were no longer there.
paragraphs.source_literal: He looked-back, but of-woman and of-campfire there already not was.

questions.prompt: Why did the man not notice that the path had come to an end?
choices: It was already dark.
He was thinking about his life.
He was talking to his friend.
questions.explanation: 'Ду́маючи про своє́ життя́, він не помі́тив...' The imperfective participle names what he was doing at the same time.

questions.prompt: Why did he sing as he walked toward the fire?
choices: So as not to be afraid
To call his friend
Because he had found the path
questions.explanation: 'Ідучи́ на вого́нь, він ти́хо співа́в, щоб не боя́тися.' 'Щоб' with an infinitive gives the purpose.

questions.prompt: Where was his friend's house, according to the old woman?
choices: Next to the campfire
At the top of a mountain
Across the river
questions.explanation: She says 'Ха́та ва́шого дру́га за рі́чкою.' 'За' with the instrumental means behind or beyond.

questions.prompt: What did the man see when he looked back?
choices: The woman was waving to him.
His friend was coming toward him.
Neither the woman nor the fire was there.
questions.explanation: 'Жі́нки й вогни́ща там уже́ не було́.' 'Не було́' with the genitive says that something was not there, and 'уже́' adds 'no longer'.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian words with their English meanings
Match each verb with its meaning

choices: The path goes to the summit.
The path goes to the river.
The path goes through the forest.

exercises.prompt: The Ukrainian name 'дієприслі́вник' joins the names of two parts of speech. Which two?
choices: the noun and the adjective
the verb and the adjective
the verb and the adverb
exercises.explanation: It joins 'дієсло́во', verb, and 'прислі́вник', adverb: the form is a verb form that does an adverb's job in the sentence.

exercises.audio_target: Ідучи́ до па́рку, Тара́с зустрі́в Се́ма.
choices: On his way to the park, Taras met Sam.
On his way to the park, Taras called Sam.
On his way to the station, Taras met Sam.

exercises.prompt: Which form is the imperfective adverbial participle of 'чита́ти'?
choices: чита́ють
чита́ючи
прочита́вши
exercises.explanation: Drop '-ть' from the 'вони́' form 'чита́ють' and add '-чи': 'чита́ючи'. 'Прочита́вши' is the perfective form, from 'прочита́ти'.

exercises.prompt: Which form is the adverbial participle of the perfective verb 'поверну́тися'?
choices: поверта́ючись
поверну́вся
поверну́вшись
exercises.explanation: The masculine past is 'поверну́вся'. Drop '-ся', add '-ши' and then '-сь': 'поверну́вшись'. 'Поверта́ючись' comes from the imperfective 'поверта́тися'.

choices: Climbing the mountain, Olena got lost.
Coming down the mountain, Oksana got lost.
Coming down the mountain, Olena got lost.

exercises.prompt: In 'Ідучи́ додо́му, Окса́на поба́чила Тара́са.', who was walking home?
choices: Oksana
Taras
Both of them
exercises.explanation: The action of an adverbial participle always belongs to the subject of the main verb. The subject of 'поба́чила' is Oksana, so she was walking home.

exercises.prompt: 'Прочита́вши нови́ни, Тара́с пішо́в на робо́ту.' When did Taras go to work?
choices: While he was reading the news
After he had read the news
Before he read the news
exercises.explanation: A perfective adverbial participle names an action completed before the main verb: first he read the news, then he left.

exercises.hint_source: Taras sang as he climbed the mountain.
exercises.explanation: The climbing happens at the same time as the singing, so the imperfective form is needed: the 'вони́' form 'підніма́ються' without '-ся' is 'підніма́ють'; drop '-ть', add '-чи' and then '-сь'.

exercises.hint_source: Having read the message, Oksana smiled.
exercises.explanation: She read the message first and smiled afterward, so the perfective form is needed: 'прочита́в' plus '-ши'.

exercises.hint_source: Taras works while listening to music.
exercises.explanation: Two actions at the same time with one subject: 'слу́хають' minus '-ть', plus '-чи'. 'Му́зику' stays in the accusative, as after 'слу́хати'.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'ї́дучи' stressed on its first syllable but 'ідучи́' on its last?
choices: 'Ї' always carries the stress of a word.
Each keeps the pattern of its 'вони́' form: 'ї́дуть' stresses the stem, and 'іду́ть' stresses the ending, so the stress moves to '-чи'.
'Ідучи́' is perfective, and perfective forms stress the ending.
exercises.explanation: Both are imperfective. The stress follows the 'вони́' form: 'ї́дуть', 'ї́дучи'; 'іду́ть', 'ідучи́'.

exercises.hint_source: Having come back home, we drank tea.
exercises.explanation: Coming home was completed before the tea, so the perfective form is needed: 'поверну́вшись' from 'поверну́вся', 'прийшо́вши' from 'прийшо́в', or 'приї́хавши' from 'приї́хав' for coming by vehicle.

choices: The '-ся' of 'посміха́тися' takes its short form '-сь' in an adverbial participle.
'-сь' marks a past action.
'-сь' shows that the subject is a woman.
exercises.explanation: An adverbial participle of a reflexive verb ends in '-сь': 'посміха́ючись', 'озира́ючись', 'поверну́вшись'. The form never shows gender or tense.

exercises.prompt_target: Оле́на ви́йшла з кімна́ти, нічо́го не ___.
exercises.hint_source: Olena left the room without saying anything.
exercises.explanation: 'Не' with an adverbial participle means 'without doing': the perfective 'не сказа́вши' or the imperfective 'не ка́жучи'. 'Нічо́го' and 'не' make the double negative.

exercises.hint_source: Being a doctor, Olena knows what to do.
exercises.explanation: 'Бу́ти' builds its adverbial participle on the future 'бу́дуть': 'бу́дучи'. The noun after it is in the instrumental, 'лі́каркою'.

choices: [ʋ], as at the start of 'вода́'
[w], because it stands before the consonant 'ш'
It is not pronounced.
exercises.explanation: 'В' before a consonant is said [w], as in 'вже': [prɔt͡ʃɪˈtɑwʃɪ]. Every form in '-вши' has this [w].

exercises.prompt_source: Oksana smiled as she listened to the song.
She went out without looking back.
Having rested, we went down to the river.
Having found the path, Olena went home.
exercises.explanation: Finding the path came first, so the perfective form 'знайшо́вши', from 'знайшо́в', is used, set off by commas wherever it stands.

exercises.prompt_source: Coming down the mountain, Sam noticed a tent.
answers: Спуска́ючись із гори́, Сем помі́тив наме́т.
Сем помі́тив наме́т, спуска́ючись із гори́.
Сем, спуска́ючись із гори́, помі́тив наме́т.
exercises.explanation: Going down and noticing happen at the same time, so the imperfective 'спуска́ючись' is used. 'Із' stands between the consonants of 'спуска́ючись' and 'гори́'.

exercises.prompt_source: When Taras was reading, Oksana was singing.
exercises.explanation: The two actions have different subjects, so an adverbial participle cannot be used. A clause with 'коли́' or 'по́ки' gives each action its own subject.

exercises.prompt_source: To tell the truth, I got lost.
exercises.explanation: 'Пра́вду ка́жучи' is a fixed phrase, common in conversation, set off by a comma. The past agrees with the speaker: 'заблука́в' for a man, 'заблука́ла' for a woman.

exercises.hint_source: We were slowly climbing the mountain.

exercises.audio_target: Купи́вши квитки́, ми пої́хали на вокза́л.
exercises.hint_source: Having bought the tickets, we went to the station.

exercises.audio_target: У рюкзаку́ є хліб і вода́.
exercises.hint_source: There is bread and water in the backpack.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, why does Taras tell Sam to take a warm jacket?
choices: Sam has no jacket of his own.
It is going to rain on Saturday.
It is very cold in the mountains at night.
exercises.explanation: Taras says 'бо в гора́х уночі́ ду́же хо́лодно': because it is very cold in the mountains at night.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, how did Olena find the path again?
choices: She heard the river, walked to it and found the path there.
She phoned Oksana, who explained the way.
She waited until morning and followed other walkers.
exercises.explanation: She stood still and heard the river: 'Дійшо́вши до рі́чки, я знайшла́ сте́жку.' Her phone did not work there.

exercises.prompt: Oksana is telling a friend about her evening over coffee. Which sentence is the most typical of conversation?
choices: Прийшо́вши додо́му, я подзвони́ла Се́мові.
Я подзвони́ла Се́мові, прийшо́вши додо́му.
Коли́ я прийшла́ додо́му, я подзвони́ла Се́мові.
exercises.explanation: All three are correct, but conversation usually prefers a clause with 'коли́' to an adverbial participle, which belongs mainly to writing.
